courseTitle: Physics 2: Fluids, Heat, Electricity, Light and Atoms
title: Magnetic Flux
short: Φ = BA cos θ counts the field passing through a loop, with θ measured from the loop's normal.
trouble: Students measure the angle from the loop's plane instead of its normal.

blocks.html: Faraday's discovery, coming up next, depends on one quantity: how much magnetic field passes through a loop of wire. That amount is the magnetic flux. It uses the cosine from Sine, Cosine and Tangent and the field you met in Magnetic Fields and Their Sources.

For a flat loop of area $A$ in a uniform field $B$, $$\Phi = BA\cos\theta,$$ where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the loop's normal (the line sticking straight out of the loop). The unit is the weber: $1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T·m}^2$.

Think of field lines as rain and the loop as a hoop. Held flat under the rain, the hoop catches the most. Tilted, it catches less, because the area it shows to the rain shrinks to $A\cos\theta$. Held edge-on, it catches none. The flux counts field lines the same way: $B$ times the area facing the field.

blocks.name: ph-induction

opts.task: Find the angle that makes the flux zero, and the angle that makes it largest.

blocks.cap: Tilt the loop. The flux is largest at $\theta = 0$, when the field passes straight through, and zero at $90^\circ$, when the loop lies along the field.

blocks.html: Measuring $\theta$ from the plane of the loop instead of from its normal. If a problem says "the field makes $30^\circ$ with the plane of the loop", the angle from the normal is $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$. Quick check: a field lying in the loop's plane must give zero flux, and $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ does that.

blocks.title: A tilted loop
blocks.q: A loop of area $0.050\ \text{m}^2$ sits in a $0.40\ \text{T}$ field. Its normal is $60^\circ$ from the field. Find the flux.

blocks.title: Angle from the plane
blocks.q: A circular loop of radius $0.10\ \text{m}$ is in a $0.20\ \text{T}$ field that makes $30^\circ$ with the plane of the loop. Find the flux.

blocks.html: A coil of $N$ turns has the same flux through each turn, so the total, $N\Phi$, is $N$ times bigger. You will use that in Faraday's law.
